16331-new-york-times-current-history-the:
This volume of New York Times Current History gathers documents and comment from the European War's first months. A statement approved by Dr. Dernburg, dated November 1, 1914, argues that Austria-Hungary and Russia, whose differences sharpened for years, made the struggle unavoidable after the Sarajevo tragedy. Germany and France, tied by alliances, joined them, while Italy and England, each tied to one side yet removed from the continent, faced uncertain choices.

Current History gave American readers the war in documents, maps, and essays as it unfolded. The volume preserves German, Allied, and neutral voices side by side. Students of the First World War will find a valuable contemporary record of how the war was explained.
23646-the-pharaoh-and-the-priest-an-hist:
Alexander Glovatski's historical novel of ancient Egypt reached English readers in 1902 through Jeremiah Curtin, translator of Quo Vadis and With Fire and Sword. Its setting is the Nile valley, where every acre of rich soil was laid down by river mud from inner Africa, and where grain from Egyptian fields fed Rome, Greece, and Judaea.

That wealth could only be worked by a whole people directed together. The novel's conflict grows from that fact: the pharaoh and the priesthood, the two powers that commanded the land's labor, contend for control of Egypt. Curtin prefaces the tale with an essay on Egypt's unique place, making this both a romance of the ancient world and a study of power built on the river.
30772-minutes-of-the-proceedings-of-the-:
Held here are the minutes of the second convention of delegates from the abolition societies of the United States, held at Philadelphia from January 7 to January 14, 1795. Printed by Zachariah Poulson Jr. on Chestnut Street, the minutes open at City Hall on Wednesday, January 7, 1795, following a convention held in the city the year before. Delegates came with credentials from societies across the young republic.

Connecticut sent Jonathan Edwards, Uriah Tracy, and Zephaniah Swift, while New York and Pennsylvania sent men such as William Rawle, Benjamin Rush, Samuel Coates, and Caspar Wistar. The minutes record who sat, what was moved, and how the societies joined their efforts against slavery. It is a primary source for early American abolition, plain in form and rich in names and dates.
31315-charles-sumner-centenary-historica:
Archibald H. Grimké's 1911 address, number fourteen in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, marks the centenary of Charles Sumner. The Academy celebrated on Friday evening, January 6, 1911, at Washington's Fifteenth Street Presbyterian Church, with a choir singing A Mighty Fortress, an invocation by the Reverend L. Z. Johnson, Grimké's historical address, a brief address by Justice Wendell Phillips Stafford, a solo by Dr. Charles Sumner Wormley, an address by Vice-President Kelly Miller, a poem by Mrs. F. J. Grimke, and a closing address by William E. Chandler.

Grimké opens with the fable of Hercules receiving sword, bow, breastplate, and robe from the gods, arguing Sumner likewise drew strength from many sources. Sumner loved the science of law rather than its practice, thirsting for permanent principles in Grotius, Pothier, Mansfield, and Blackstone. The address honors a statesman as the Academy's own hero.
31323-the-demand-and-the-supply-of-incre:
Jesse E. Moorland's 1909 paper, number thirteen in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, argues for a greater number of efficient ministers. Moorland concedes a Christian lawyer or doctor holds as genuine a divine calling as any minister, with such men stressing service over gain. He calls the minister's efficiency probably the most important question confronting colored people.

A race or nation, he argues, is measured by its religion, and the Negro minister has been responsible both for the race's progress and for much that cannot count as progress. No other class, he notes, holds so large and far-reaching an influence. The paper tells the familiar anecdote of Queen Victoria holding up the Bible as the secret of Britain's greatness, and pleads for well-trained, honorable, upright ministers in every community.
doe-osti-17198173-nonlinear-data-compres:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-27128R, printed in September 2026, presents R. Loek Van Heyningen's work on shrinking simulation data by first aligning it. The method, called image registration, learns a smooth, reversible warp of the domain so that moving features in separate simulation fields line up. Aligned fields can then be squeezed into a small set of basis patterns, which cheaper reduced models are trained on.

Two approaches are developed for bounded domains, where the warp must not distort the shape of the domain. One builds the map from radial basis functions in a layered, composed scheme that guards the boundary. The other follows a vector flow with a constrained kernel that limits which maps are allowed. Both are tested on two- and three-dimensional transient problems and on steady aerodynamic data over curved and non-convex domains.
doe-osti-3002144-tasti-grid-overview-of-:
Hillary Fishler, Varisara Tansakul, and Supriya Chinthavali of Oak Ridge present a slide deck, ORNL/LTR-2025/4000, on Oregon's power grid. The deck introduces TASTI-GRID, a national tool that helps states and tribes decide where grid resilience money does the most good. It draws on more than 60 public data sets. Oregon is the worked example here.

Slides map Oregon's generation and transmission lines, substations, past major outages, and extreme weather impacts. Other slides cover customer demographics, meter types, and whether energy rates stay affordable. The deck closes with steps for small towns and rural cooperatives, such as gradual metering upgrades with incentives. State energy offices use this kind of overview before they commit funds to harden the grid against storms.
doe-osti-3097328-los-alamos-innovation-e:
Los Alamos National Laboratory tells a tech transfer story in report LA-UR-26-23101, issued April 15, 2026, under Dharmesh N. Patel. Lab researchers built a porous sorbent that pulls carbon dioxide from air with little energy. A firm named Spiritus licensed the material, which anchors its Carbon Orchard approach to direct air capture. The sorbent now sits at the heart of a much larger build-out planned in Wyoming.

Spiritus joined a 500 million dollar partnership with Prometheus Hyperscale and Casper Carbon Capture. Their Casper, Wyoming project pairs permanent carbon removal with advanced computing plants, billing the result as one of the largest carbon-negative digital infrastructure projects in the world. The sheet frames the deal as proof that lab materials work can scale into heavy industry.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaserGreg_Raser: Greg Raser wrote this letter by hand to Harold Weisberg in April 1994. Handwritten letters fill the later years of Weisberg's mail, from readers and researchers who had followed his books for decades. The file keeps the letter under Raser's name and its date. It does not summarize what Raser wrote, so the letter's news or requests cannot honestly be described beyond its place in that correspondence.
new-york-times-current-history-the-europ:
The New York Times issued this number of its Current History magazine on the European War. It covers the start of the war to March 1915. Its theme is set as a question: Who Began the War, and Why? The contents begin with the case for Germany.

Speeches by Kaiser Wilhelm the Second fill much of the number. He forgives enemies, speaks from the throne, and addresses the German army and navy. Other pieces cheer the men as one for the Kaiser, hearts for God and fists on the enemy. His letter to Lord Tweedmouth is also printed. Readers in America could weigh Germany's own words early in the war.
podcast-tuckercarlson-JS-3QssVPeg:
Economist Jeffrey Sachs joins Tucker Carlson to give what the title calls the untold history. It covers the Cold War as he reconstructs it, and the CIA coups that punctuated it around the world. It also covers the origin of Covid. On that subject Sachs has broken publicly with the official account he once helped administer.

Sachs chaired the Lancet's Covid commission and emerged convinced the virus likely came from laboratory work, a position he argues here alongside his longer indictment of American foreign policy. Carlson, an eager host for both arguments, lets him build the full arc. Sachs's views are contested by many former colleagues; his standing makes the contest significant. The episode preserves a pillar of the establishment prosecuting the establishment, in detail, which is a rarer document than any outsider's critique.
